# Umbraco Rules

Project conventions, enforced by code in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco` where possible. The short version of the ten UmbraCommandments.

1. **Never put content behind a composition.** Removing a composition permanently deletes its content on every document that used it — no recovery through revisions. Compositions are for meta, settings, CTAs. Litmus test: *if we remove this composition later, is what remains still viable content?*
2. **There are six kinds of document type — file each in its folder.** Page (renders), Block (renders; lives in block list/grid; never used as a composition), Composition (composed onto others; never rendered, never pickable), Data (element; never renders — settings, events, people), Repository (container node; never renders), Repository Item (the pickable records inside a Repository).
3. **Data types never sit at the root of the data type tree.** Built-ins under `/Umbraco/<editor>`, custom ones under `/Custom/<editor>`. `DataTypeSavedHandler` enforces this on every save.
4. **Register in an `IComposer`, not Program.cs.** If `IUmbracoBuilder` can do it, it belongs in `Composers/`. Non-Umbraco concerns (CORS, App Insights) go in `WebApplicationBuilder` extension methods.
5. **Production runs in production mode.** Umbraco Application Url set, `--configuration Release`, HTTPS only, no model generation, no template editing. `appsettings.json` ships configured this way — don't soften it; put dev conveniences in `appsettings.Development.json`.
6. **Aliases are English and camelCase.** No exceptions.
7. **Dictionary keys are PascalCase with dots** (`My.Dictionary.Item`), and a dictionary folder never has values of its own.
8. **Media always lives in a folder.**
9. **The content root only holds Repositories.** The site hangs under the WWW `siteRoot` node; going multi-site means adding another Page beneath it, not re-architecting. Because WWW never renders, the site Page needs a **domain** or nothing answers on `/` — assign `/` for a single site, a hostname each for several.
10. **uSync everything — commit `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/uSync/`.** Export is automatic; you should not need to trigger it. On Umbraco Cloud, use Umbraco Deploy instead.

A model with tools can act: query the CMS, read a file, publish a page. MCP hands those capabilities over in a structured, discoverable way — the model finds the tool, reads its description and calls it correctly, usually on the first try.

It is the difference between a chat window and a colleague.

It makes integrations boring

"Boring" is the highest compliment for infrastructure. MCP turned "build an integration" into "list your tools in a JSON schema" — a weekend job instead of a quarter.

Every boring integration is one more capability the model gets for free, everywhere it runs.

It keeps the humans in charge

MCP draws the line cleanly: the server owns what is possible, the model decides when, and the person confirms whether. Capability is described explicitly, so reviewing what an assistant could do is as easy as reading its tool list.

That is a safety model you can explain to a non-developer — which is exactly what a protocol needs to be.

values.value: This blog post is the demo

value.markup:
Everything on this page was created through the Umbraco MCP servers: the document types behind it, the block grid you are reading, the images in the media library — and this very post.

No migrations were written by hand, no database was touched, no backoffice was opened. The protocol did all of it, which is the most convincing argument for MCP I can think of.

Content modeling over the wire

The Umbraco MCP server exposes the same primitives an editor uses: document types, data types, templates, media. Composing those into a site from a conversation turns schema work from a deployment task into a dialogue — describe the structure you want, inspect what exists, adjust.

The guardrails matter as much as the reach: mutations are explicit, validation happens server-side, and the site's own rules are enforced on every call. An assistant that can only do what the tools allow is an assistant you can trust with a production CMS.

Why it clicks with a CMS

A CMS is already a tool server at heart: it has entities, permissions and an audit trail. Mapping MCP onto that is natural — the protocol becomes the universal remote for content operations.

The result is an editing experience where "make me a blog" is a request you can actually make. Not a demo trick: the same tools that created this page can update it tomorrow, safely, under the same permissions.
